findings.title: Negative-offset branch is unreachable / raises AssertionError in Django
findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset < 0. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that a slice start must be non-negative (`assert (k.start is None or k.start >= 0), 'Negative indexing is not supported.'`), so this branch raises AssertionError in normal Python and produces undefined SQL offsets under python -O. Cursor.from_string happily parses a negative offset via `int(bits[1])`, so an admin who sends ?optimized_pagination=true with a crafted cursor (e.g. '0:-5:0') will crash the endpoint. The claim in the comment that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong; Django never supported negative slicing on querysets.

findings.title: 'Performance optimization' comments are misleading
findings.body: The block comment at lines 179-181 and the docstring of OptimizedCursorPaginator (lines 822-832) claim this is a 'performance optimization', provides 'efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning', 'streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'optimized query path for large datasets'. None of these are real. Compared to BasePaginator, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result only changes behavior when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, and even that change is broken (see the negative-offset finding). The change to BasePaginator itself (line 182-184) only clamps a negative offset to 0 in the non-prev case; that is a defensive fix, not an optimization. The repeated blank lines at lines 819-820 also suggest the class was tacked on without review.

findings.title: has_global_access on RpcOrganizationMember is not a known attribute
findings.body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` accesses a Python attribute on the RpcOrganizationMember RPC type. RpcOrganizationMember typically exposes role/flags (e.g. `flags.global_access` bit) rather than a `has_global_access` property. If the attribute does not exist, this expression raises AttributeError on every request from a non-superuser, which would 500 the entire audit log endpoint for ordinary members. The reviewer needs to confirm the actual attribute name and that it represents the intended privilege (vs. e.g. `role` or a flags bit). Also, since the entire `use_optimized and enable_advanced` branch is gated to superusers or admins, exposing it via a user-controlled `?optimized_pagination=true` query parameter does not actually grant any new capability and should be questioned.

findings.title: New paginator branch has no tests
findings.body: No tests were added for the new optimized_pagination code path. A maintainer should at minimum cover: (1) optimized_pagination=true with a superuser hits OptimizedCursorPaginator; (2) optimized_pagination=true with a regular member falls through to DateTimePaginator; (3) OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True and a negative-offset cursor does not raise (today it will). The whole feature is unverified.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (lines 845-911) is an almost line-for-line copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 136-215); the only meaningful difference is the negative-offset branch. Subclassing only to flip one branch in one method duplicates ~70 lines of cursor/offset/extra/hits/post_query_filter logic. Any future fix to BasePaginator (including the pre-existing `order_b` typo on line 105) must be made in two places. A maintainer would prefer a single `enable_advanced_features` flag on BasePaginator, or an override of just the slicing step.

findings.title: Pre-existing typo 'order_b' silently breaks ASC re-ordering
findings.body: Pre-existing but in the file being changed and directly relevant to pagination correctness. Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` instead of `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`. This means when the cursor's key is currently ordered DESC (`-%s` % self.key in order_by) and `asc` is True, the queryset's order_by is never actually flipped to ascending, so the descending-order rows are then compared with an ascending comparison operator, producing wrong results. Worth fixing while this file is being touched.
